examples.question_text: Sketch $y=3\sin(2x)$ for $0\le x\le\pi$. Use horizontal lines to determine the number of solutions of: a. $3\sin(2x)=\frac32$; b. $3\sin(2x)=3$; c. $3\sin(2x)=4$. Find the exact solutions for part a.
Sketch each side on the same axes and find the exact intersection $x$-coordinates: a. $3\cos(2x)+1=\frac52$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$; b. $2\tan\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)=2\sqrt3$ for $0\le x\le4\pi$.

The function $f(x)=4\cos\left(\frac{\pi x}{5}\right)+2$ has period $10$ and a minimum at $x=5$. One solution of $f(x)=4$ is $x=\frac53$. Use symmetry and the period to find all solutions in $0\le x\le20$.
By sketching $y=\sin x$ and $y=\frac{x}{2}$, determine how many real solutions $\sin x=\frac{x}{2}$ has and how many are positive. Show algebraically that every solution lies in $-2\le x\le2$.
By drawing both graphs, determine how many real solutions $\cos x=\left|\frac{x-\pi}{5}\right|$ has. Explain why your sketch includes every possible intersection.

Sketch $y=1+\sin\left(\frac{\pi x}{3}\right)$ for $0\le x\le6$. By considering lines through the origin, find the values of $m$ for which $\sin\left(\frac{\pi x}{3}\right)=mx-1$ has exactly one solution in this domain.

examples.derivation: With u=2x, the domain becomes [0,2π]. sin u=1/2 gives u=π/6,5π/6, hence x=π/12,5π/12. The maximum 3 occurs only at x=π/4; height 4 exceeds the range [-3,3]. The plotted intersections agree.

For part a, cos(2x)=1/2 and 0≤2x≤4π give x=π/6,5π/6,7π/6,11π/6. For part b, tan(x/2)=√3 and 0≤x/2≤2π give x=2π/3,8π/3. The tangent asymptotes are x=π,3π. Both plots and their marked intersections match these results.

At x=5/3, cos(πx/5)=cos(π/3)=1/2, so f(x)=4. Reflection about x=5 gives 10−5/3=25/3. Adding period 10 gives 35/3 and 55/3. These are all four intersections in [0,20]. The two bare-expression continuation blocks have correctly aligned phantom equals gutters.

The sine range requires −1≤x/2≤1, hence −2≤x≤2. On (0,2), sin x−x/2 is strictly concave, initially increasing and negative at x=2, giving exactly one positive root. Odd symmetry gives one negative root, alongside x=0. The plotted nonzero roots ±1.895494 and heights ±0.947747 agree.

An intersection requires |x−π|≤5. In this interval, cosine can be non-negative only on the lobes around 0 and 2π. On the first lobe, cos x−(π−x)/5 is negative at both lobe endpoints and positive at x=0; strict concavity gives exactly two crossings. Reflection about x=π gives two more on the other arm. The plotted V has the correct vertex, slopes and height-one bounds.

The curve has maximum (3/2,2), minimum (9/2,0) and endpoint (6,1). Negative gradients give no intersection; m=0 gives only the trough. For m>0, concavity on [0,3] and decreasing curve height on [3,9/2] give exactly one crossing before the trough. Afterwards, the curve-minus-line is strictly convex, starts negative and ends at 1−6m, giving one additional crossing exactly when 0<m≤1/6. Thus exactly one solution occurs for m=0 or m>1/6. The plotted boundary and representative steeper line agree.
